title: Learner Needs Analysis

points.sub: What will they actually use English for?
pts: Start from the target situation: where, with whom, and for what purpose will the learner use English?
A syllabus built on assumed needs, not real ones, wastes classroom time on the wrong priorities.
ESP and EAP contexts make this explicit; general English contexts still need it, just implicitly.
points.who: John Munby, "Communicative Syllabus Design"; Hutchinson & Waters, "English for Specific Purposes"

v: Twelve situation cards per group (see model language); a large sheet of paper per group

items: Put learners in groups of four. Give each group twelve situation cards, face down.
Groups turn the cards over and sort them into three piles: ‘I do this in English now’, ‘I will do this in English in the future’, ‘Not for me’.
Each group chooses its top three ‘future’ cards and writes them on the sheet, with one reason each.
Groups present their top three. Tally the class results on the board.

For homework, each learner interviews one adult who uses English (a relative, a neighbour, a shopkeeper) with three questions: ‘Where do you use English? What is hard? What do you wish you had learned at school?’
Next lesson, add the interview answers to the tally. The top five situations become priority topics for the term.
With adults in work-related courses, replace the cards with the learners’ own job tasks written on sticky notes.
With younger learners (11–12), use picture cards and ask only ‘Now’ or ‘Later’.
Support: give the three interview questions in both English and the class’s shared home language.
Stretch: learners write a short report, ‘What English does my uncle need?’, comparing two interviews.

lines: Reading a science textbook / Filling in a form at a bank / Talking to a tourist / Watching a cricket match in English / Writing an email for a job / Answering a board examination paper / Using a phone app in English / Reading medicine instructions / Chatting online with a cousin abroad / Giving directions / Speaking at an interview / Reading a newspaper
S1: I think writing an email for a job is important because we will all need jobs.
S2: I agree. And reading a science textbook is important now.

body: Purpose: to show the sorting activity at a glance. Content: three wide columns headed with icons: a clock showing now (‘Now’), an arrow pointing forward (‘Future’), and a cross (‘Not for me’). Under each, four small card shapes with short labels from the list above, drawn as if tossed slightly askew. Style: friendly, flat colours, readable at A5. Board version: three columns with words.

items: Mentimeter (free basic version). Put the twelve situations in a multiple-choice question and let each learner choose their top three on a phone. The results appear as a live bar chart for step 4.

blocks.x: Tally by show of hands, or give each learner three small stones or paper dots to place on the situations written on the board.

Munby’s model (1978) listed hundreds of categories for describing a learner’s communicative needs. It was criticized for being too detailed to use in practice, but its central question, ‘What will these learners actually do with English?’, remains the starting point for most course design.

pts: Placement testing answers "which class?" — a single overall score sorting learners into groups.
Diagnostic testing answers "which gaps?" — a skill-by-skill profile guiding individual attention.
Treating one test as both wastes its most useful information.

v: 50 minutes (can be split over two lessons)
Four short tasks, one per skill; a class profile grid

items: Prepare four short tasks of about eight minutes each: a listening task (the teacher reads a short announcement twice; learners answer four questions), a reading task (a short notice with four questions), a writing task (a four-sentence note to a friend) and a speaking task (a one-minute picture description to the teacher or a trained peer).
Explain clearly that this is not a test with a grade. ‘It helps me plan lessons for you.’
Run the tasks. In a large class, do listening, reading and writing as a whole class; do speaking in small groups over the next week while others work on a reading task.
Score each task on a simple 0–3 scale (0: not yet; 1: some; 2: most; 3: all, easily).
Transfer scores to a class grid (Figure 2.2). Look for patterns across the class and within each learner.
If you already have placement results, use the diagnostic only for the skill that placement did not test (often speaking).
With young learners, replace the writing task with ‘draw and label’.
Support: read reading-task questions aloud for learners with low literacy in English, so that you test reading of the text, not of the questions.
Stretch: add an optional extra question to each task at a higher level.

blocks.x: Placement and diagnosis ask different questions:

lines: Placement: ‘Which class should this learner join?’ → one overall score.
Diagnosis: ‘What exactly does this learner need next?’ → a profile across skills.
Asha: Listening 3, Reading 3, Writing 1, Speaking 2. She understands well but struggles to put ideas on paper. Priority: guided writing with models (Unit 3, point 7).

body: Purpose: a photocopiable record sheet (Appendix). Content: a table with learners’ names down the left and four columns (Listening, Reading, Writing, Speaking), each cell holding a score 0–3, with a final ‘Notes’ column. Beside it, a mini bar chart for one learner showing four bars of different heights. Style: ruled grid, 10 pt, shading light for column heads. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Forms quiz mode (free). Set up the listening and reading tasks as auto-marked quizzes. The ‘Insights’ view shows which questions most learners got wrong, which is itself diagnostic.

blocks.x: A paper grid kept at the front of the register. Colour-code cells with pencil: red 0–1, yellow 2, green 3. Patterns become visible at a glance.

body: Tell learners what the diagnostic is for, and then show them their own profile. Learners who see that their listening is strong and their writing is weak have a reason to work on writing, which a single mark never gives them.

pts: Record L1 background, prior instruction, literacy in L1, and exposure outside class.
Age and educational background change how explicit grammar instruction should be.
A profile updated across the course, not just at intake, keeps planning responsive.

v: 30 minutes, then five minutes every few weeks
A folded A4 ‘passport’ per learner (see Appendix); learners’ language portraits from Unit 1

items: Show a real passport or its picture. Explain that each learner will make an ‘English passport’ that records who they are as a learner.
Learners complete page 1: name, languages (from their portrait), where they meet English outside school.
Page 2: ‘How I learned English so far’, with prompts: school since Grade…, English-medium or not, tuition, apps, films.
Page 3: ‘What helps me learn’ and ‘What is hard for me’.
The teacher adds page 4 privately: diagnostic scores (point 2), notes on reading and writing in the home language, any known additional needs.
Every four to six weeks, learners add a ‘stamp’: one new thing they can do in English, dated.
For adults, add ‘Education and work background’ and ‘Time available for study each week’.
For young learners, the teacher fills in page 2 from a short conversation.
Support: allow answers in the home language on pages 2 and 3.
Stretch: learners write a short ‘learner biography’ paragraph as page 5.

blocks.x: Why literacy in the home language matters: a learner who reads fluently in Kannada already knows how reading works (predicting, sounding out, rereading). A learner who is not yet confident reading in any language needs a different start. Profile entry, page 3:

lines: What helps me: When the teacher writes on the board. When my friend explains in Telugu.
What is hard: Speaking in front of the class. Spelling.

body: Purpose: to show the folded booklet. Content: an A4 sheet folded twice into a small booklet. Cover: ‘My English Passport’ with a globe icon and a space for a photo or drawing. Inside pages shown open: headings ‘Me and my languages’, ‘My English story’, ‘What helps me / What is hard’, and a page of empty stamp circles labelled with dates. Style: warm, simple, printable in one colour. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Docs or Microsoft Word template stored in a shared class folder, one copy per learner, so that profiles can be updated from any device.

blocks.x: Paper passports kept in a box file or large envelope in the classroom. The box travels with the teacher; the passports stay with the class.

pts: Instrumental motivation (a job, an exam) and integrative motivation (belonging to a community) call for different classroom incentives.
Dörnyei's "Ideal L2 Self" reframes motivation as the gap between who a learner is and who they want to become in English.
Ask directly — motivation is one of the few needs a simple conversation can surface well.
points.who: Gardner & Lambert; Zoltán Dörnyei's L2 Motivational Self System

v: Quiet space; paper; optional soft background music

items: Ask learners to close their eyes (or look down) for two minutes. Guide a short visualization: ‘It is five years from now. You are using English easily. Where are you? Who are you speaking to? What are you doing?’
Learners open their eyes and write notes: place, people, activity, feeling.
Learners write a short letter from their future self to their present self: ‘Dear me, I am writing from…’
In pairs, learners share one sentence from their letter.
Collect or ask learners to keep the letters in their passports. Revisit them when motivation dips (see Unit 47).
If visualization feels uncomfortable for a group, replace step 1 with a picture prompt: learners choose a photo that represents ‘me using English in the future’.
For adults, add a practical second half: ‘Three steps to get there this year’.
Support: provide the letter frame (see model language).
Stretch: include one sentence about a difficulty their future self overcame.

blocks.x: Instrumental and integrative motivation (Gardner and Lambert 1972):

lines: Instrumental: I need English to get a job in a hospital.
Integrative: I want to make friends with people from other countries.
Dear me, I am writing from ______. I am ______ (doing what?). I use English to ______. The hardest thing was ______, but I ______.

body: Figure 2.4 Two selves and the gap between them

Purpose: to show Dörnyei’s idea of the ideal L2 self simply. Content: two figures on a path. Left figure labelled ‘Me now’, holding a small book. Right figure labelled ‘Ideal English-using me’, speaking confidently in a scene (an office, a hospital, a stage). Between them, stepping stones labelled ‘practice’, ‘feedback’, ‘small wins’. Style: gentle, optimistic, two-colour line art. Board version: two stick figures and stones.

items: FutureMe (free website). Learners who have email can send the letter to themselves, to be delivered on a chosen date, for example at the end of the school year. [VERIFY current service terms and age requirements before use with under-18s.]

blocks.x: Seal the letters in envelopes addressed by each learner to themselves and return them at the end of the year.

body: Ask a class: ‘Why are you learning English?’ Record the answers as they come, without comment. Then ask: ‘Why do you want to learn English?’ The second question often produces very different, more personal answers, and those are the ones worth planning around.

pts: The idea that matching instruction to a "visual" or "auditory" style improves outcomes has failed every controlled test.
What does help: teaching multiple strategies explicitly and letting learners choose what works per task.
Replace style labels with strategy inventories that track what a learner actually does when studying.
points.who: Pashler et al. (2008) meta-analysis; Rebecca Oxford's Strategy Inventory for Language Learning

v: Three sets of ten words at the same level; a short test for each

items: Explain the experiment: ‘We are going to try three ways of learning words and see which works for us.’
Session 1 (look and copy). Learners copy set A three times with translations.
Session 2 (test yourself). Learners study set B, then cover the English and try to recall it from the translation, repeating until they get all ten.
Session 3 (use it). Learners write a sentence about themselves with each word from set C.
Two days after each session, give a short recall test. Learners record their scores in a table.
Discuss: which strategy worked best for most people? For you? Most classes find that testing themselves and using words outperform copying, whatever learners believed about their ‘style’.
Add a fourth strategy that learners propose themselves.
With younger learners, use five words per set.
Support: choose simpler words for the whole class rather than a separate list, so the comparison stays fair.
Stretch: learners design their own ‘fair test’ for a new strategy.

blocks.x: The strategy table after the experiment:

lines: Copying: average 4/10 / Self-testing: average 7/10 / Using in sentences: average 7/10 (illustrative figures; your class’s results will differ).

blocks.x: What to say instead of ‘learning styles’:

lines: Not: You’re a visual learner, so look at the pictures.
Instead: Pictures help everyone remember new words. Try covering the word and saying it from the picture.

body: Purpose: to replace a familiar myth with a practical alternative. Content: on the left, three crossed-out badges reading ‘visual’, ‘auditory’, ‘kinaesthetic’. An arrow leads right to a toolbox containing labelled tools: ‘self-test’, ‘space it out’, ‘use it in a sentence’, ‘picture + word’, ‘say it aloud’. Style: clean, slightly playful; the toolbox is the visual focus. Board version: three crossed-out words and a list.

items: Quizlet (free basic version) or Anki (free on desktop and Android). Both build self-testing into the practice, which is the strategy research supports most consistently.

blocks.x: Paper flashcards with the English word on one side and a picture or translation on the other. Learners test themselves in pairs.

body: A widely cited review by Pashler and colleagues (2008) found no adequate evidence that matching teaching to a learner’s preferred ‘style’ improves learning. People do have preferences; the evidence simply does not show that teaching to them helps.

pts: CEFR can-do statements describe what a learner can do, not an abstract score — "can follow the main points of a discussion."
Self-assessment against can-do checklists is often more accurate than learners guessing a level number.
Use can-do descriptors to set the aim of Unit 9's lesson plans, not just to sort classes.
points.who: Council of Europe, CEFR Companion Volume

v: A ladder handout with eight can-do statements at rising levels (write your own, based on the CEFR scales)

items: Draw a ladder on the board. Explain that each rung is something people can do in English, from easy to hard.
Give out the ladder handout. Read each statement aloud and check understanding with a quick example.
Learners mark each rung: ✓✓ (I can do this easily), ✓ (I can do this with help), ✗ (not yet).
In pairs, learners show each other one ✓✓ statement by doing it: for example, introducing themselves.
Collect the ladders. Compare them with the diagnostic results from point 2. Where they differ sharply, talk to the learner.
Use the lowest ✓ rungs across the class to choose next week’s lesson aims.
Make separate ladders for speaking and for writing.
Repeat the ladder every term and let learners see how their marks have moved.
Support: provide the statements with a picture or an example beside each one.
Stretch: learners write a new rung between two existing ones.

blocks.x: Sample ladder statements (written for this book, based on the style of the CEFR scales):

lines: I can say my name, age and where I live. (A1)
I can ask for simple things in a shop. (A1–A2)
I can describe my family and my school in a few sentences. (A2)
I can follow the main points of a short announcement. (A2)
I can tell a simple story about something that happened to me. (A2–B1)
I can give my opinion and a reason in a discussion. (B1)

body: Purpose: a photocopiable self-assessment sheet. Content: a tall ladder with eight rungs. Beside each rung, a statement and three small tick boxes (✓✓ / ✓ / ✗). At the top, a small flag labelled ‘B1’; at the bottom, ‘A1’. Style: one colour, generous spacing, 11 pt statements. Board version: a ladder with rung numbers only.

items: Google Forms with a grid question (rows: statements; columns: ✓✓ / ✓ / ✗). The summary view shows the class picture instantly.

blocks.x: The paper ladder, kept in the learner’s passport. Learners colour the rungs they have reached, a little like a growth chart.

pts: Some learners arrive ready to self-direct; others expect the teacher to make every decision — both are legitimate starting points.
Autonomy readiness affects how much homework, self-study, and choice a course can realistically ask for.
Build autonomy gradually rather than assuming it, especially with learners new to communicative classrooms.
points.who: Henri Holec, "Autonomy and Foreign Language Learning"

v: A2–B1 (instructions in home language if needed)
A line drawn on the floor or board from ‘The teacher decides’ to ‘I decide’; six statement cards

items: Draw the line. Read the first statement card: ‘Which words I learn this week.’
Learners place a sticky note, a chalk mark, or themselves along the line to show who they think should decide.
Discuss briefly: why did people choose different places?
Repeat for the other five statements (how I practise, when I do homework, what I read, how I check my work, what my learning goal is).
Note where most learners stand. Choose one area where the class is closest to ‘I decide’ and offer a real choice next week.
As a written questionnaire with a five-point scale for each statement.
With adults, add ‘how much time I can spend studying each week’.
Support: pair learners so no one stands alone at an extreme.
Stretch: learners explain in two sentences why they chose their position.

lines: Week 1: choose which of two reading texts to read.
Week 3: choose five words from the text to learn.
Week 6: choose how to practise them and report back.

body: Purpose: to visualize the continuum. Content: a long horizontal line with a teacher figure at the left end and a learner figure at the right end. Six labelled markers along it (words, practice, homework, reading, checking, goals), each with a small cluster of dots showing where a class might stand. Style: minimal, two colours. Board version: line, two stick figures and dots.

items: Mentimeter or Slido (free basic versions). A ‘scale’ question shows the average position of the class for each statement.

blocks.x: A human line: learners stand in the room between two signs, which also gets a restless class moving for a few minutes.

pts: Initial needs analysis is a hypothesis, not a verdict — revisit it once real classroom behaviour gives better evidence.
Short, ongoing check-ins catch shifting goals that a one-off intake form misses.
Treat the learner profile as a living document you edit across the course, not a file you archive after week one.
points.who: Ian Tudor, "The Dynamics of the Language Classroom"

v: Three columns on the board or slips of paper

items: Draw three columns: ‘Stop’, ‘Start’, ‘Continue’.
Learners write one idea for each on a slip, anonymously: something in our English lessons we should stop, start or continue doing.
Collect the slips. Read a selection aloud without names.
Tell learners one thing you will change as a result, and when.
Keep the slips. Compare them with next month’s. Update learner profiles (point 3) where individual needs have changed.
With young learners, use faces: ☺ ‘more of this’, ☹ ‘less of this’.
Run it as a two-minute ‘one-word check-in’ at the start of a lesson: ‘One word for how English feels this week.’
Support: accept answers in any language.
Stretch: learners suggest how to make their ‘start’ idea work.

blocks.x: Typical slips and what they tell you:

lines: Stop: Reading aloud one by one. → Anxiety about public reading (see Unit 22).
Start: English songs. → Motivation and listening interest.
Continue: Group work on Fridays. → A routine that works.

body: Purpose: to show that needs analysis is ongoing. Content: a circle of four arrows labelled ‘Find out’, ‘Plan’, ‘Teach’, ‘Check again’, with small icons (a magnifying glass, a notebook, a board, a speech bubble). In the centre, ‘Learner profile’. Style: clean circular diagram, one accent colour. Board version: four words in a circle with arrows.

items: Google Forms with three short-answer questions, collected anonymously each month.

blocks.x: Slips in a box, as in the activity.

dek: Unit 2 of 100: before a single lesson is planned, find out who is in the room — their goals, gaps, motivation and readiness — and let that evidence drive every decision that follows.

aims.x: This unit turns the first foundation of Unit 1, ‘Know your learner’, into a practical toolkit. It shows how to find out what learners need English for, what they can already do, why they are learning, and how ready they are to learn on their own, and how to keep that picture up to date.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: describe the target situations in which your learners will use English;
explain the difference between placement and diagnostic testing and choose the right one;
build and maintain a simple learner profile for every learner in a class;
identify learners’ motivations and use them in planning;
replace ‘learning styles’ labels with evidence-based strategy work;
use can-do statements for placement, self-assessment and lesson aims;
judge how much independent study a class is ready for.

why: Why this matters. Every tool in this series — from PPP grammar staging to task design — is only as good as the profile of the learner it's aimed at. Skip this step and even excellent methodology misses its target.

background.x: Needs analysis sounds like a job for a curriculum office, and in large programmes it often is. But every teacher does a version of it, usually without naming it, in the first week of a new class. The difference between a guess and a needs analysis is simply that the second is deliberate: it asks specific questions, records the answers and uses them.

The term grew up in the 1970s, when teachers of English for specific purposes began asking what an engineer, a pilot or a nurse actually needed to do in English. John Munby’s Communicative Syllabus Design (1978) proposed a highly detailed model for answering that question. Later writers, notably Tom Hutchinson and Alan Waters (1987), argued that learners’ needs include not only what they must do at the end of a course (the target situation) but what they need in order to learn along the way: time, confidence, materials and a reason to keep going. This unit uses both ideas.

Needs analysis matters just as much in general English. A class of fourteen-year-olds in a government school has needs too: to pass a board examination, to understand the English in their science textbooks, to follow a cricket commentary, to chat with a cousin in Dubai. Their needs are less visible than a nurse’s, which is precisely why they are easy to ignore.

In multilingual settings, a needs analysis should also map the languages learners already have. The National Curriculum Framework for School Education (NCERT 2023) plans for learners studying three languages, often referred to as R1, R2 and R3, and treats the home language as the foundation for the others. Knowing which languages a class shares tells a teacher which bridges are available for explaining new English.

items: Profile completeness. Check that every learner has a passport with pages 1–4 completed within the first month.
Self-assessment accuracy. Compare can-do ladder marks with diagnostic scores. Learners whose self-assessment is far above or below their performance may need a conversation about confidence.
Motivation follow-up. Midway through the term, ask learners to reread their future-self letters and write one sentence about progress towards it.
Strategy uptake. After the ‘three ways’ experiment, check vocabulary notebooks two weeks later: are learners using self-testing?
What do you currently know about why each of your learners is learning English? How did you find out?
Have you ever used a placement result as if it were a diagnostic? What information was missing?
Where did your own belief in ‘learning styles’, if you had one, come from? What would change if you set it aside?
Which decisions in your classroom could learners make for themselves next month?
How often do you revise your view of a class after the first few weeks? What prompts you to do so?

perm: The ladder statements are original paraphrases in the style of the CEFR. Any direct quotation of CEFR descriptors must be acknowledged to the Council of Europe; check current terms for commercial reuse.

Screenshots of Mentimeter, Slido, Google Forms, Quizlet or FutureMe require permission from the rights holders or must be replaced by original illustrations. Any use of a real passport image in Figure 2.3 must be avoided; the artwork should be a clearly invented design.

terms.def: A description of what a learner can do in a language, as in the CEFR, used for setting goals, self-assessment and describing levels; for example, ‘I can write a short email inviting a friend.’
A test designed to identify learners’ specific strengths and weaknesses in order to plan teaching; contrast a placement test, which assigns learners to a level.
The image of the person a learner would like to become as a user of the second language, such as a confident English-speaking engineer. It is a key source of motivation (Dörnyei 2009).
Motivation to learn a language for practical benefits, such as passing an examination or getting a job (Gardner and Lambert 1972).
Motivation to learn a language because of interest in, or a wish to connect with, its speakers and their culture (Gardner and Lambert 1972).

The capacity to take charge of one’s own learning, including setting goals, choosing materials and methods, and evaluating progress (Holec 1981); it is developed gradually, through guided choices, rather than simply handed over.
A simple record of an individual learner’s background, languages, interests, level and needs, built up at the start of a course and updated over time to guide planning and support.

The specific actions and techniques learners use to make learning easier and more effective, such as guessing meaning from context, grouping vocabulary or planning before speaking (Oxford 1990); many can be taught explicitly.

Learners’ supposed preferred ways of taking in information, such as visual or auditory; research has not shown that matching teaching to a learner’s style improves learning, so varied, multimodal teaching is the safer choice.
The systematic gathering of information about why learners need English, what they must do with it, and what they already know, to guide course design and lesson planning.
A test used at the start of a course to place learners in the group or level best suited to their current proficiency.

Learners judging their own performance or progress against criteria, for example with ‘can do’ statements or a checklist. It builds awareness, responsibility and autonomy, and gives the teacher useful information.
The real-world context in which learners will need to use English, such as a workplace, college course or travel. Describing it clarifies what learners must be able to do and guides course planning.
